keyList.text: The ISA manual defines cpop in the Zbb extension: population count of the source register. Zbb is an extension, not base ISA, so its presence varies by chip.
The lab's disassembly check verifies the compiler did not replace the SWAR mask sequence with a cpop instruction (the POPCNT shortcut), so the two sides of the comparison are genuinely independent.
The lab's method depends on the two sides of the comparison staying on opposite sides of the instruction/emulation boundary.
If the compiler silently emits cpop for the SWAR code, the differential test becomes circular, cpop tested against cpop, and proves nothing. Crossing the boundary unknowingly is the failure mode.
The complementary failure mode is assuming cpop where Zbb is absent: the instruction raises an illegal-instruction trap on chips without the extension.

The working tools for this boundary are the ISA manual (which extension owns the instruction), the disassembler (what the compiler actually emitted), and QEMU with extensions toggled (does it trap without Zbb).
A layer matters to a lab when the lab's method depends on a boundary that layer defines and the characteristic failure modes live at that boundary.
The lab ran on an x86_64 host and never executed a RISC-V instruction, so one could argue no RISC-V ISA is involved.

The lab's method is about the boundary, not about where each side ran: the differential test needs the two sides to stay independent, and the disassembly check enforces that. The ISA manual defines which instructions exist and which extension carries them, so asking whether the compiler crossed the boundary is an ISA question even though the run happened on a host. Real-hardware execution would add timing, which is a microarchitecture question, not an ISA one.

The SWAR routine is plain C over uint64_t built only from the 0x5555/0x3333/0x0F0F mask identities: no inline assembly, no compiler intrinsics, no ISA-specific operations.
C unsigned integer arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N on every conforming implementation, so identities built only on unsigned arithmetic and shifts hold identically on every ISA at the same word width.
The routine's behavior is fixed by C unsigned arithmetic, not by any ISA feature.
The failure mode of a portability claim is hidden ISA dependence: an assumption the proof needed but never stated. Stating word width and wraparound up front is the defense.
